chapters.title: Chapter 3: Reading a Deal as an Investor

lessons.title: Merger Arbitrage: Reading the Spread Between Swap Value and Market Price

children.text: Zee Entertainment's merger with Sony's Indian business was announced in December 2021 and sanctioned by the NCLT in August 2023. By then, many investors treated it as a done deal. On 22 January 2024, Sony terminated the merger agreement. On the next trading day, Zee's shares fell more than 25%. Anyone who had bought Zee to pocket the gap between its price and the value of a completed merger learned the central lesson of merger arbitrage the hard way: the gap exists because the deal might not happen.

body.text: The merger arbitrage spread is the market's price for waiting and for the risk that the deal breaks. Buying the spread is not collecting free money. It is selling insurance against deal failure: you earn a small, steady premium if the deal closes and take a large loss if it does not.

children.text: What the Spread Is
In Lesson 2.2 you calculated the implied value of a target share: swap ratio × the acquirer's current price. Pending targets almost always trade a little below that implied value. The gap is the
arbitrage spread
Merger arbitrage
is the strategy of trying to earn it.

markDefs.definition: The difference between what a target share will be worth if the deal completes, such as the implied value in a share swap or the offer price in a cash deal, and its current market price.
An event-driven strategy of buying shares of a company being acquired, often while hedging exposure to the acquirer, to earn the spread when the deal completes.

body.latex: \text{Spread (\%)} = \frac{\text{Value if deal completes} - \text{Target's market price}}{\text{Target's market price}} \times 100
body.caption: For a share swap, value if the deal completes is swap ratio × acquirer's price. For a cash offer, it is the offer price.

children.text: The spread exists for three reasons. First, money is tied up until the deal closes, often for many months, and could otherwise earn a return in a fixed deposit or liquid fund. Second, the deal might fail. Third, many investors, especially funds with restrictions, sell targets after announcement rather than wait, which pushes the price slightly below fair value.
Worked Example: The Malabar Coatings Spread

Back to our fictional merger from Lesson 2.2: Malabar Coatings is merging into Konkan Paints at 437 Konkan shares for every 1,000 Malabar shares. Today Konkan trades at ₹520 and Malabar at ₹218. The deal is expected to close in 8 months.
Implied value of a Malabar share = 0.437 × ₹520 = ₹227.24.
Spread in rupees = ₹227.24 minus ₹218 = ₹9.24.
Spread in percent = ₹9.24 ÷ ₹218 × 100 = 4.24%.

body.caption: A simple annualisation, good enough to compare with a fixed deposit or liquid fund yield.

body.title: Annualise the Malabar spread
body.prompt: The Malabar spread is 4.24% and the deal is expected to close in 8 months. What is the approximate annualised spread? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 4.24% × 12 ÷ 8 = 4.24% × 1.5 = 6.36% a year. That is roughly what a bank fixed deposit pays, except the FD does not carry the risk of the merger collapsing. On these numbers, the spread is not paying much for the risk.

body.text: Timelines slip. If the Malabar deal takes 14 months instead of 8, the same 4.24% spread annualises to only about 3.6%. Delays from regulators, NCLT hearing dates or objections are common in India, so always test your return assuming the deal takes longer than management says.

children.text: The Lopsided Payoff
Now ask what happens if the deal breaks. Before the announcement, Malabar traded at around ₹190, and without the merger it would likely fall back towards that level.

The spread also tells you what probability the market assigns to the deal completing. Ignoring the time value of money, today's price should equal the probability-weighted average of the two outcomes.

body.latex: \text{Implied probability} = \frac{\text{Market price} - \text{Price if deal fails}}{\text{Value if deal completes} - \text{Price if deal fails}}
body.caption: Derived from: Market price = p × Value if completes + (1 − p) × Price if fails.

body.title: What probability is the market pricing in?
body.prompt: Malabar trades at ₹218, would be worth ₹227.24 if the deal completes and about ₹190 if it fails. What probability of completion is the market implying? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (₹218 minus ₹190) ÷ (₹227.24 minus ₹190) = ₹28 ÷ ₹37.24 = 0.7519, or about 75.2%. If you believe the true probability is 95%, the spread looks attractive. If you think this deal has a real chance of failing, it does not. Arbitrage is a bet on your probability estimate versus the market's.

body.title: How a spread usually behaves when the deal is on track

body.text: A spread that narrows steadily is the market growing more confident and running out of waiting time. A spread that suddenly widens is a signal: the market has spotted a new risk, such as a regulator's query, a shareholder revolt or a dispute between the parties. Treat a sudden widening as news to investigate, not a bargain to buy.

children.text: When Deals Break

body.title: Zee Entertainment and Sony: a scheme that was sanctioned and still failed

events.title: Merger agreement signed

body.caption: What can break a deal after it is announced

cells: SEBI, RBI, CCI or a sector regulator refuses or delays approval
Queries in the observation letter, CCI's detailed investigation
Negative proxy advisor reports, large institutions opposing
A party walks away when a closing condition is not met by a deadline
Long-stop dates approaching, disputes over conditions
Investigations, litigation or promoter issues derail the deal
SEBI orders, court cases, auditor resignations
The acquirer cannot raise the money for a cash deal
Rising leverage, falling acquirer share price, tight credit

body.title: Read the signal
body.question: A fictional pending merger has traded at a steady 2% spread for months. One morning, with no announcement from either company, the spread jumps to 9%. What is the most sensible interpretation?
options: A free opportunity, because the deal terms have not changed
The market is pricing in a higher chance of the deal failing or being delayed, so you should find out why before acting
The acquirer must have raised the swap ratio
Spreads move randomly and carry no information
body.explanation: When terms are unchanged and the spread widens sharply, someone is selling the target because they believe the risk of failure or delay has risen. Check exchange filings, regulator orders, court listings and news before assuming the market is wrong.

children.text: Share Swap vs Cash Deal Arbitrage

columns.label: Share swap spread
points: Value if completed moves daily with the acquirer's share price
Professionals buy the target and short the acquirer in the swap ratio to lock in the spread
An unhedged investor is exposed to the acquirer's price falling
Typical of schemes of arrangement, such as HDFC and HDFC Bank

columns.label: Cash offer spread
points: Value if completed is a fixed rupee offer price
No hedge needed against the acquirer's price
In oversubscribed open offers, only part of your shares may be accepted
Typical of open offers, delisting offers and buybacks

body.title: Can a retail investor in India hedge a share swap?

children.text: In the Indian cash market, you cannot hold a short position overnight, so the hedge has to come through stock futures. That creates practical problems.
The acquirer must be in the NSE F&O segment. Many mid-cap and small-cap acquirers are not.
Lot sizes are fixed, so matching the swap ratio exactly usually needs a large target holding.
Futures expire monthly, so the short must be rolled repeatedly, with a cost each time, for a deal that may take a year.
Margin is blocked for the whole period, and profits or losses on futures are taxed as business income, while gains on the target shares are capital gains. The two do not always offset neatly for tax.
For most retail investors, buying the target without a hedge is not arbitrage at all. It is simply a leveraged bet on the acquirer's share price plus the deal closing.

body.title: Name the gap
body.textWithBlank: The difference between a target's value if the deal completes and its current market price is called the arbitrage ___.
body.explanation: The spread compensates for waiting and for the risk that the deal fails. It narrows as completion approaches and widens when risks rise.

body.title: The "safe 5%"
body.scenario: Your colleague has ₹5 lakh in a fixed deposit earning 7%. He reads that a fictional target, Kaveri Logistics, trades 5% below the implied value of its pending all-stock merger into a large listed acquirer, with completion expected in 6 months. He plans to break the FD and put the full ₹5 lakh into Kaveri Logistics shares, calling it "a safe 10% a year".
body.prompt: What would you point out before he does this?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Annualised, 5% over 6 months is about 10%, but only if the deal closes on time. If it takes 12 months, it is about 5%, below his FD.
2. It is not safe. If the deal breaks, Kaveri could fall back to its pre-announcement price, which may be 15% to 30% lower. Ask what it traded at before the announcement to size that loss.
3. It is unhedged. Without shorting the acquirer, a 10% fall in the acquirer's price cuts his value by about 10%, wiping out the spread twice over.
4. Implied probability: estimate what failure probability the 5% spread reflects, and whether he has any real edge in judging it.
5. Concentration: putting his entire emergency or savings money into one event-driven position is the bigger mistake, whatever the spread.
6. Taxes and costs: breaking the FD may carry a penalty, and gains on Kaveri shares held under 12 months are short-term capital gains.
7. A more sensible approach, if he still wants exposure, is a small position he can afford to lose a quarter of.

body.title: Before buying a pending target for the spread
steps: Calculate the implied value and spread using today's acquirer price
Annualise the spread using a realistic, not optimistic, completion date
Find the target's pre-announcement price to estimate the loss if the deal breaks
Work out the implied probability of completion and compare it with your own view
List the approvals and conditions still outstanding, including long-stop dates
Decide how you will handle exposure to the acquirer's share price
Keep the position small enough that a broken deal does not hurt your overall portfolio badly

body.label: NSE India
body.description: Check whether an acquirer is in the F&O segment, its futures lot size and the monthly expiry dates before thinking about a hedge.

cards.definition: Buying a target's shares after a deal announcement, often hedged, to earn the spread when the deal completes.
Value if the deal completes minus the target's market price.
The spread scaled to a yearly rate, roughly spread × 12 ÷ months to completion.
(Market price minus price if the deal fails) ÷ (value if the deal completes minus price if it fails).
The risk that a deal fails, sending the target back towards its pre-announcement price.
The deadline in a merger agreement by which conditions must be met, after which a party can terminate.

points: Pending targets trade below the value of a completed deal. That gap is the arbitrage spread.
The spread pays for waiting and for the risk the deal breaks, so it is closer to selling insurance than to free money.
The payoff is lopsided: a small gain if the deal closes, a large fall back to the standalone price if it does not.
Implied probability = (market price minus fail price) ÷ (complete value minus fail price). Your view must beat the market's to justify the trade.
Deals can die even after NCLT sanction: Zee's merger with Sony was terminated in January 2024, and Zee's shares fell more than 25% the next day.
In India, hedging a share swap needs stock futures, which brings lot size, rollover, margin and tax complications for retail investors.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Konkan Paints, Malabar Coatings, Kaveri Logistics and the investors in the examples are fictional. Details of the Zee and Sony merger are from public disclosures and news reports. Merger arbitrage involves significant risk of loss, and derivatives trading carries additional risks. Mentioning a company is not a recommendation to buy or sell its shares.
